content:
Councillor Mike Sole, Cabinet Member for
Finance introduced the report that sets out the proposed changes to
charges and conditions in the Off-Street Parking Places Order
(OSPPO) for the financial year 26/27 and includes the
results of the public consultation and the views of the Overview
Committee. 
 
The Cabinet discussed the report, and the
Cabinet Member gave clarification where necessary. 
 
Members supported the report and
the proposals and discussed points that
included: 
 

Minimal parking
charge increases were proposed, with some
car parks having remained at the
same level for the third successive
year.  


There was evidence
that residents and visitors were starting to
change their behaviour and use
alternative cheaper parking outside of the city
centre. 


The situation in
Herne Bay and Whitstable differed to
Canterbury with weather factors playing a
part and less range of available parking
options. 


Some free parking was
trialled there during the winter which had been
successful and would be reviewed. 


The consultation
responses would be useful in the body of evidence for the
Local Plan/Transport Strategy.  


The carbon
saving calculation was welcomed. Members
discussed how the coach
parking experience could be improved in the
future.  


There was feedback
from workers who were unhappy paying for parking
when working in the city. Links with businesses
and increased publicity of car sharing and Park
& Ride were discussed. 



Members discussed linking more closely with
universities to encourage students to use Park
& Ride. 



Members expressed a preference for a whole
district strategy covering a longer period if
possible. 

 
It was then proposed, seconded and when put to
vote RESOLVED: 
 

That item numbers 1-4, as set out
in Appendix 1 and 2, are implemented on 1st April
2026. 

 
 
Record of the voting:  
 
For (9): Councillors Baldock, Castle,
Charlotte Cornell, Chris Cornell, Dawkins, Hazelton,
Nolan, Ricketts and Sole  
Against (0): None  
Abstained (0): None 
 
Reason for decision: 
 

The proposals help to
meet objectives of transport, parking and climate change
strategies that encourage greater use of sustainable transport and
Park & Ride  


Additional income raised will
help to reduce the council’s overall funding gap
and maintain essential services.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to implement proposed changes to parking charges for the financial year 26/27.

content:
Councillor Chris Cornell, Cabinet Member
for Economic Development and Inclusion introduced
the report and city and town centre strategies for
Canterbury, Herne Bay and Whitstable that seeks Cabinet
approval to adopt appendices A, B & C. 
 
Option 1: Adopt the city and town centre
strategies for Canterbury, Herne Bay and
Whitstable.  
 
Option 2: Adopt the city and town centre
strategies for Canterbury, Herne Bay and Whitstable with
amendments. This would delay the adoption of these strategies and
mean the opportunity to integrate them into the Local Plan prior to
adoption could be lost.  
 
Option 3: Do not adopt the city and town
centre strategies for Canterbury, Herne Bay and
Whitstable. 
 
The Cabinet discussed the report and
strategies, and the Cabinet Member gave clarification where
necessary and discussed points that included: 
 

Appreciation was expressed to
officers, consultants, Cabinet Members, and all
contributors for developing clear, engaging and forward?looking
strategies within tight timeframes. 


Links were noted between this
item and the earlier discussion on parking. 


It was acknowledged that trading
conditions are challenging. The role of creating high streets
that felt engaging and welcoming was
emphasised.  


The importance of
consistency was highlighted and having a clear sense of
what the council is aiming to achieve. Members reaffirmed that
this is intentionally a long?term plan. 


Minor amendments to
wording would be made to outcomes 1, 8 and 10 of the
Canterbury City Strategy outcome section.  


Seeing all elements come together
highlighted the importance of the work, particularly in relation to
the Local Plan. 


Members observed that the
area has long suffered from a lack of high?quality
accommodation and expressed hope that more conference
accommodation may come forward and suggested exploring
links to accommodation in nearby areas. 


Clarification was given that
adopting the strategies established the governance
framework for a long?term plan. 


The importance of the next
section was noted, particularly around populating directories
with ideas. Regular progress updates would be provided to
Cabinet. 


Councillor Carnac’s
comments would be included as part of the debate when
forming panels and taking the work forward. 


The strategies would be
positioned as a key vision document that aligned with the
Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) and would help shape the
organisation’s identity going forward. 


Members agreed that building
momentum over the next two years was essential as the
work transitions into the first year of unitary authority
arrangements. 


Cabinet welcomed and were fully
supportive of the adoption of the City and Town Centre Strategies
that highlighted both the challenges and opportunities. 

 
 
 It was then proposed, seconded and when
put to vote RESOLVED: 
 

That the city and town centre
strategies for Canterbury, Herne Bay and Whitstable
(appendices A, B & C) are adopted. 

 
Record of the voting:  
 
For (9): Councillors Baldock, Castle,
Charlotte Cornell, Chris Cornell, Dawkins, Hazelton,
Nolan, Ricketts and Sole  
Against (0): None  
Abstained (0): None 
 
Reason for decision:  
 

To anchor a single, evidence?led
framework for our urban centres, aligned with the draft Local Plan
and shaped through wide engagement.  


Adoption provides clear direction
and continuity through local government reorganisation, giving
partners and investors a stable, shared basis for
decisions.  


The strategies focus delivery on
tangible outcomes tracked and sequenced via a project directory and
18?month action plans to maintain momentum.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to adopt city and town centre strategies for Canterbury, Herne Bay, and Whitstable.

This council acknowledges the acute

negative impact of sewage pollution on local
communities. 


This Council acknowledges that
additional housebuilding will increase the strain on local water
infrastructure and wastewater treatment capacity. 


This Council will continue to exert
pressure on water companies, water regulators, and all other
relevant agencies, to help address these concerns. 


This Council will also seek actions
and potential solutions that it can implement to help tackle the
problem. 


With this in
mind, this Council urges the Cabinet to commission an urgent
report into the viability of implementing the so-called Wealden
planning condition and other strategy options as tools for tackling
the problem of sewage pollution in this district.

Leader of the Council to write to Steve Reed, the Secretary of
State for Housing, Communities and Local Government, asking him to
accept Amendment 197 to the Water & Infrastructure Bill. This
amendment ends the automatic right of water companies to connect to
the foul drainage system and ensures developers must prove to
independent Sustainable Drainage Advisory Boards that they have a
plan for wastewater drainage.

content:
The Chief Executive Officer of Partnership One
introduced the report and business plan. He explained that
PartnershipOne’s vision statement
and Strategic Plan, which set out six goals that would enable the
achievement of that vision over three years, had already been
approved. 
 
The Business Plan set out activities and areas
of focus against each enabling goal for the first year, with a
strong focus on four themes around stability: workforce,
operational, service and financial. A key theme for this year was
embedding the new LATCO’s culture and building trust. Output
performance on core services was measured through six Key
Performance Indicators (KPIs) for each of the three
partners.  
 
Councillors discussed the report, asked
questions and clarified points, including the following: 
 

Local Government reorganisation
could present both a threat and an opportunity for PartnershipOne. The company’s core team
had extensive experience of on-boarding cultural alignment and
still delivering excellent services. The company’s aim to
deliver such good services that it could be a valid contender to
continue to provider those services
under the new unitary council, and perhaps for other unitaries. Ownership of the business would transfer
to the new council entity. 


Once there was clarity on the
geographical boundaries of the new unitary council, the company
would be able to develop delivery options. PartnershipOne would be a strong candidate offering
continuity of good service, so customers would not notice the
difference.    


Concerning the IT costs on page 23
of the agenda: under the previous arrangement with Civica, the
councils owned the IT. Under this arrangement, the IT was owned by
PartnershipOne, so the costs were new
to the company but pre-existing within the
councils.  


Councillors commended the activity
under Goal 6 (added social value) which in Year 1 would be around
maximising discretionary awards for residents and the wider
involvement in community activities through the ‘donate a
day’ scheme.  


The Business Plan was generally
written in clear, accessible language, although a little editing
was needed on page 3 [of the business plan]. 


Performance (both KPIs measuring
outputs and activities contributing to outcomes) would be reported
on monthly to the company’s Board of
Directors.  


The Year 2 Business plan would need
to come to the Committee for sign off, and that would also be an
opportunity for an early look at Year 1 performance. A date for
this meeting would be advised in due course.   

 
It was proposed, seconded and 
 
RESOLVED
 
unanimously by general assent:
 
To Recommend to the Cabinets of Canterbury
City Council, Dover District Council and Thanet District Council
that the 2025/26 Business Plan for PartnershipOne be approved.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to recommend the approval of the 2025/26 Business Plan for PartnershipOne to three district councils.

content:
Councilllor Charlotte Cornell introduced the report
that outlined the methodology of developing a new Cultural Strategy
including review of the achievements from the previous strategy and
stakeholder engagement. It accompanied the draft Cultural Strategy
2026-2036 and requested permission to move to public consultation
to ensure the final strategy reflects the ambitions of the council,
its partners and the wider public.  
 
Cabinet were
asked to consider the following options: 
 
Option 1 – Open
public consultation before the adoption of the Cultural Strategy
2026-2036 
Option 2 – Move
straight to the adoption of the Cultural Strategy 2026–2036
without consultation 
Option 3 –
Extend the use of the Cultural Recovery Strategy as the strategic
framework.
 
The Cabinet discussed the report
and the following points were made: 
 

The Cabinet discussed the establishment of a
district-wide cultural forum to support the ongoing maintenance of
the strategy and to ensure that the council remained accountable to
its ambitions. 


Cabinet noted ongoing partnership work, including
a prospective UNESCO City of Literature bid (end of 2026), with
festivals in Whitstable, literature and storytelling in Canterbury,
and music creation supporting a vibrant Herne
Bay. 


It was noted that extensive consultations had
already taken place with many stakeholders, and that the strategy
would be further reviewed by the Overview Committee to gather
additional input from councillors. 


The potential to include grassroots music venues
located in towns, villages, and cities, as well as rehearsal
spaces, was also considered. 


Members emphasised the
importance of maintaining flexibility within the strategy,
recognising that culture continually
evolves. 


A request was made that the villages be better
reflected in the introductory section, citing notable cultural
connections (e.g., Henry Moore, Joseph Conrad, Ian Fleming,
Mozart/Bishopsbourne).  


The Cabinet noted the role of village halls and
pubs as cultural spaces and rehearsal
opportunities 


District-wide participation was encouraged through
comments online or directly to Members. 

 
It was proposed, seconded and when put to a recorded vote
RESOLVED: 
 
To open public consultation prior to the adoption of the
Cultural Strategy 2026-2036.
 
Record of the voting: 
For: Councillors Baldock, Sole, Castle, Charlotte Cornell, Chris
Cornell, Dawkins, Hazelton, Ricketts (8) 
Against: None 
Abstained: None 
 
Reason for decision: 
To provide opportunity to adopt a strategy that has been
codesigned with the sector through broad public
engagement.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to open public consultation before adopting the Cultural Strategy 2026-2036.

content:
Councillor Pip Hazelton introduced the report that
updated Cabinet on the recent inspection undertaken by the
Regulator of Social Housing against the Consumer Standards, pending
the issue of the outcome of the regulatory judgement and
grading. 
 
A service improvement plan had been drafted and would be amended once the feedback from the
Regulator of Social Housing is received and asked Cabinet to
consider setting up a Cabinet Advisory Committee to act as a
critical friend.
  
Cabinet were being asked to consider the following
options: 

Option 1 –
Create a Cabinet Committee  
Option 2 –
Create a Cabinet Advisory Committee  
Option 3 –
Create a Cabinet Working Group/Task and Finish Group
 
Option 4 –
Create a Scrutiny Sub Committee 
 
The Cabinet discussed the report
and the following points were made: 
 

Officers had already been working towards a
service improvement plan, regardless of the outcome from the
housing inspection. 


The Cabinet emphasised
that political oversight and tenant involvement were considered
critical. 


Members expressed hope that the first meeting of
the Cabinet Advisory Committee (CAC) would take place by the end of
October. 


It was noted that the committee would be
politically balanced, with the Cabinet Member for Housing acting as
Chair, and that the frequency of meetings could be adjusted
depending on the outcome of the inspection. 


Although it was thought there could be some grey
area of overlap with the companies advisory committee, it was
confirmed that the two are very different, and that this option
allows for co-opting tenant representatives. 


It was confirmed that the creation of this
committee would not have an impact on existing task and finish groups. 


Officers clarified that tenant engagement was a
requirement of the regulator, making it essential for tenant
representatives to be involved. 


The Cabinet considered the proposed committee as a
way for scrutiny to remain informed of progress and discussed how
scrutiny could feed into committee discussions. 


Support was expressed for a smaller committee of
3-1-1-1 (politically balanced), but with a greater number of
co-opted tenant members. 


It was noted that third parties could be invited
to attend when reviewing specific areas, although their involvement
would not be required from the outset and was unlikely to be
ongoing co-option. 


Cabinet confirmed that the service improvement
plan would be amended based on the regulator's
findings. 

 
Cabinet NOTED the update in the report. 
 
It was then proposed, seconded and when put to a recorded
vote RESOLVED :  
 
To set up the Cabinet Advisory Committee as outlined in
this report. 
 
Record of the voting: 
For: Councillors Baldock, Sole, Castle, Charlotte Cornell, Chris
Cornell, Dawkins, Hazelton, Ricketts (8) 
Against: None 
Abstained: None 
 
Reason for decision: 
A
Cabinet Advisory Committee is not decision making and could act as
a critical friend offering both scrutiny and challenge. Tenants and
third-party representatives could be co-opted. The Portfolio holder could actively engage.
It provides a longer-term governance route and scrutiny, supports
transparency, and enables tenant involvement in line with
regulatory requirements.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to set up a Cabinet Advisory Committee in response to a recent inspection by the Regulator of Social Housing.

content:
The Deputy Head of the East Kent Audit
Partnership presented the report, which set out a summary of the
work of the East Kent Audit Partnership since the last Audit
Committee meeting and progress against the internal audit
plan. 
 
Four reports had been completed with assurance
levels ranging from substantial to reasonable. In addition, three
follow-up reviews had been completed. 
 
The Head of Facilities Management highlighted
that the areas of follow up review (PaternshipOne – Housing Benefit Overpayment,
PartnershipOne – Council Tax, and
Tenants’ health and Safety) now all scored
‘substantial’ or ‘reasonable’ revised
assurance levels, with the exception of
only 1 area – ‘performance management’, which was
still at ‘limited assurance’. She noted that detailed
compliance reports were reviewed by Management Team monthly, and by
Cabinet every six months. Management considered this
sufficient.
 
The Director of People noted that the coming
into force of Awaab’s Law in October 2025, which required
social landlords to investigate and fix dangerous damp and mould in
set time periods, meant that the Council would now be reporting
these performance figures too. 
 
Members then made points and clarifications,
including the following:
 

·       
Item 5 ‘setting a rule within the True Compliance
system’ had a proposed completion date of July 2025, but the
management comments indicated that at present a start and
completion date could not be set. It was clarified that this was
not something the Council could do itself. The software developer
would need to give the Council a date for this action. There was a
work-around in place, so it was being mitigated, but the software
provider would need to do the work. 

·       
On point 6 (block inspections), a programme was in place to review
block inspections using a risk-based approach,
and complete this by Jan 2026.

·       
The IT issues outlined on page 46 (PartnershipOne – housing benefit payments)
had been linked with Virtual Private Network (VPN) issues and had
not affected the timely payment of benefits.
 
The Vice-Chair thanked the report writer and
the officers for their clarifications.
 
It was proposed, seconded and when put to the
vote
 
RESOLVED 
 
that the Committee accept the results of the
internal audit work. 
 
Record of the vote:
For (5): Councillors Forrester, A Harvey,
Jones, Prentice, D Smith 
Against (0): none 
Abstaining (0): none
topline: The East Kent Audit Partnership has decided to accept the results of the internal audit work.

content:
The Director of Finance and Procurement
introduced the report, which set out how the Anti-Fraud, Bribery,
Corruption and Whistleblowing Policy had been reviewed and updated
to ensure it was strengthened and improved based on current
legislation and best practice. The draft was being shared with the
Committee for comment and approval. 
 
Members made points and clarifications,
including the following: 
 

In appendix B (page 214) there was a
list of people protected under the whistleblowing policy, but it
did not include public appointments / elected councillors. Could it
be amended to include those not protected?  


Vetting IT support chain companies
was very important for fighting cyber security threats and
potentially cyber crime. The normal
procurement process included vetting companies and IT access was
now very much restricted to outside parties. IT suppliers were not
allowed into our tenant systems area.  

 
It was proposed, seconded and when put to the
vote 
 
RESOLVED  
 
That the committee approve the updated
anti-fraud, bribery, corruption and whistle blowing
policy. 
 
Record of the vote:  
For (5): Councillors Forrester, A Harvey,
Jones, Prentice, D Smith  
Against (0): none  
Abstaining (0): none
topline: The Audit Committee has decided to approve the updated Anti-Fraud, Bribery, Corruption and Whistleblowing Policy.

content:
The Director of People introduced the reports,
which summarised the complaints made to the Local Government
Ombudsman and the Housing Ombudsman about the authority and which were concluded during the year 1
April 2024 to 31 March 2025. There had been three detailed
investigations out of 29 possibles, with two complaints upheld,
both of which fell under the housing service area. All remedies had
been actioned and training had been
improved to reduce cases of maladministration, when procedures were
not properly followed.  
 
In the previous year the Audit Committee had
asked for more detail about the findings and the cases, so
summaries on these had been included in this year’s
report.  
 
Members made points and clarifications,
including the following: 
 

It was important to recognise when
and how things had gone wrong, and then
put measures in place to put things right. The progress on this
outlined in the report was very reassuring.  


The team was thanked for working
hard to achieve the maximum for people.  


Making positive changes part of the
council’s day-to-day business was very important so that
residents could get the full benefit of service
improvements. 


It would be good if the tables
listing complaints made to the Ombudsmen could include numbers and
outcomes from previous years also, so that comparison could be made
and trends spotted.  


The complaints form included a section on what outcomes the
customer wanted, but did not ask the
customer how they thought the process could be improved. 


The Council worked with the
residents engagement panel to find out
people’s experiences when making complaints.  

 
It was proposed, seconded and when put to the
vote 
 
RESOLVED 
 
That the report be discussed and formal
response noted 
 
Record of the vote:  
For (5): Councillors Forrester, A Harvey,
Jones, Prentice, D Smith  
Against (0): none  
Abstaining (0): none
topline: The Audit Committee has decided to address complaints made to the Ombudsmen and take actions to improve procedures.
